design_detail: Reply (Matters Arising, Nature Medicine 27:1691–1692, published online 11 October 2021) by MAPP1's first author and two employees of the sponsor, answering Halvorsen, Naudet & Cristea (2021) and Burke & Blumberger (2021, Caution at psychiatry's psychedelic frontier, not read). Nine running-text paragraphs and 6 references, without new data; the third page carries contributions and competing interests. Locators count paragraphs starting on each printed page.
can_establish: How the trial's authors defended the placebo-controlled design, the comparator and the breakthrough label, and what they said about cost-effectiveness, durability and treatment guidelines.
cannot_establish: That MDMA-assisted therapy is better than, or as good as, trauma-focused psychotherapy, or that its effects last: the reply adds no data, and its durability figure comes from a pooled phase 2 follow-up that was retracted in 2024 according to Brett & Bynum (2025).

sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; sources chosen by the authors.
sample.selection_effects: Sources: the authors' own trial; the sponsor's web pages on the FDA special protocol assessment and breakthrough designation; an FDA web page; a sponsor-authored comparison with SSRIs (Feduccia et al., 2019); the sponsor's pooled phase 2 follow-up (Jerome et al., 2020); and the APA guideline.

comparison.controls: Defends MAPP1's comparator: both arms received the same psychotherapy so that MDMA's contribution could be evaluated, as regulators of medicines require; argues that no flawless comparator exists for psychedelic-assisted therapy.

outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; the reply calls blinding in psychedelic trials a tremendous challenge without giving MAPP1's own blinding data.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. Cited: 67% of phase 2 participants no longer met PTSD criteria at least 12 months after their last MDMA session (Jerome et al., 2020) (p. 1692).
analysis.selective_reporting: The reply does not report MAPP1's data on earlier therapy (Table 1 of the trial), its anecdotal blinding information or its adverse-event methods, and cites the phase 2 follow-up without noting that it was pooled and uncontrolled.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Arguments: phase 3 drug-development programmes compare a medicine with placebo, not with psychotherapies; most MAPP1 participants had had at least one psychological intervention and still had severe PTSD; no comparator is flawless; cost-effectiveness had been modelled on the phase 3 design (under review); durability must still be evaluated; the APA guideline does not use the term first-line.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The reply states that the overwhelming majority of participants had engaged in at least one psychological intervention (p. 1691, 3rd paragraph); MAPP1's Table 1 supports this for any therapy (88 of 90), but it cannot be checked for first-line trauma-focused therapy: CBT (34), EMDR (30) and prolonged exposure (1) are given without their overlap, so between 34 and 65 of 90 had at least one, CBT is not specified as trauma-focused, and the adequacy of these courses is not reported. It accepts that “blinding in psychedelic trials is a tremendous challenge, and there is no perfect solution” (p. 1691, 6th paragraph) but gives no blinding data. It offers the phase 2 follow-up as evidence of long-lasting efficacy (p. 1692), from pooled, uncontrolled data later retracted (according to Brett & Bynum, 2025). It answers the guideline point by quoting the APA panel on the incomparability of control conditions across psychotherapy and medicine trials (p. 1692), an argument that also limits MAPP1's own comparison with SSRI effect sizes.

timeline.event: Jerome et al., pooled long-term follow-up of six phase 2 trials, cited for the 67% figure; retracted in August 2024 according to Brett & Bynum (2025); not read here.
Halvorsen, Naudet & Cristea, one of the two Matters Arising answered.

Burke & Blumberger, Caution at psychiatry's psychedelic frontier (doi 10.1038/s41591-021-01524-1), the other Matters Arising answered, described in the reply as highlighting the blinding problem; not read here.
MAPP2 kept the placebo-plus-therapy design; its authors name an ongoing long-term follow-up (NCT05066282).

replication.where_it_stands: The pragmatic and psychotherapy-comparator studies the reply says are underway are not reported in the sources read, nor is the phase 3 long-term follow-up; the phase 2 durability figure it cites is no longer usable.

funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: A.C. and B.Y.-K. received salary support for full-time employment with MAPS PBC/MAPS, the trial organizer and sponsor (Competing interests, third page of the PDF). No interest is declared for J.M., although MAPP1 reports that she received funding from MAPS PBC during the conduct of the study, and that she and A.C. received personal fees or grants from the Usona Institute, unrelated to the trial.
funding.affiliations_note: University of California San Francisco and San Francisco VA Medical Center (Mitchell); MAPS PBC (Coker); MAPS (Yazar-Klosinski). All three wrote the reply.

what_would_settle_it: The phase 3 long-term follow-up with outcomes for both randomized arms; a trial against a trauma-focused psychotherapy of matched therapist time; and a trial with an active comparator and measured expectancy and blinding.

domains.note: A reply; sources chosen by the authors.
The phase 2 follow-up is cited as evidence of lasting efficacy without noting that it was pooled and uncontrolled; the trial's own data on earlier therapy are not shown.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The defence rests on the authors' trial, the sponsor's documents and sponsor-authored analyses (three of six references and two sponsor web pages).
Synergy between MDMA and psychotherapy is presented as the treatment paradigm without evidence; the closing paragraph leaves effectiveness after approval to time.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the trial's comparator, blinding and durability
domains.note: Under-represented: MAPP1's lack of a blinding assessment, the absence of controlled follow-up, and evidence on trauma-focused psychotherapy in people like the trial's participants.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The reply can be cited for the sponsor's and authors' position: that phase 3 drug trials compare against placebo, that pragmatic and psychotherapy-comparator studies should follow, and that blinding has no perfect solution. It should not be cited as evidence of durability, of prior failure of first-line psychotherapy in MAPP1's participants, or of cost-effectiveness.

key_findings.finding: The trial was designed as a pivotal phase 3 study for marketing authorization, with design agreed through an FDA special protocol assessment and EMA scientific advice.

The authors agree on the value of trauma-focused psychotherapies but say the overwhelming majority of trial participants had previously engaged in at least one psychological intervention and still met the criteria for severe PTSD, and that current options are insufficient.
key_findings.note: MAPP1 Table 1 (publisher HTML): no earlier therapy in 2 of 90; prolonged exposure 1 of 90, CBT 34, EMDR 30.

key_findings.finding: Comparison with psychological interventions is said not to be part of an EMA- or FDA-regulated phase 3 drug-development programme, although such pragmatic studies should be done to inform health policy; the breakthrough designation is explained by the FDA's criteria for a drug that may show substantial improvement over approved medications for a serious condition.

Because regulators assess medicines, both arms received the same psychotherapy to isolate MDMA's contribution; MDMA is thought to act synergistically with psychotherapy, so neither psychotherapy, placebo nor an active comparator alone is ideal; blinding in psychedelic trials is called a tremendous challenge with no perfect solution, and no flawless comparator exists.

Cost-effectiveness had been evaluated on the phase 3 design and was under review; the number of sessions needed would be studied pragmatically in the sponsor's expanded access programme; trials adding MDMA to prolonged exposure and CBT were said to be underway.
key_findings.note: No source is given for the evaluation said to be under review; the critics' 2022 model built on a phase 3 trial (Marseille, Mitchell and Kahn, 2022, as listed by Marseille & Mitchell, 2025) names among its authors J. M. Mitchell, the name of this reply's first author (editors' observation).

key_findings.finding: Durability must still be evaluated; phase 3 follow-up data were being collected; previous phase 2 studies showed 67% of participants not meeting PTSD criteria at least 12 months after their last MDMA session (reference 5, Jerome et al., 2020).

The authors quote the APA guideline panel: it does not recommend psychotherapy before or instead of medicines, nor use the term first-line, because the systematic review behind the guideline found insufficient evidence from direct comparisons of psychotherapy with medicines; as an implication, efficacy inferences for the two classes may not be comparable, because their trials use control conditions of different stringency.
Competing interests: A.C. and B.Y.-K. received salary support for full-time employment with MAPS PBC/MAPS, the trial organizer and sponsor; none declared for J.M.

reporting_issues.issue: The competing-interests statement lists only the two sponsor employees; MAPP1 reports that the first author received funding from MAPS PBC during the conduct of the study, and that she and A.C. received personal fees or grants from the Usona Institute, unrelated to the trial.
reporting_issues.page: third page of the PDF (Competing interests); MAPP1, publisher HTML (Competing interests)
reporting_issues.consequence: Incomplete declaration relative to the original article.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'replying to' line spells Naudet as Naude; post-traumatic is misspelled in the 2nd paragraph; references 2 and 3 give no DOI or pages.

disagreements.first_pass: The authors quote the APA guideline panel as not recommending psychotherapy before or instead of medicines, nor using the term first-line, because psychotherapy and medicine trials use control conditions of different stringency.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 34: corrected. The quoted panel gives as its reason the lack of evidence from direct comparisons; the different stringency of the control conditions is offered as the implication, not as the reason.

disagreements.first_pass: MAPP1's Table 1 supports this for any therapy (88 of 90) but not for first-line trauma-focused therapy (prolonged exposure 1 of 90, CBT 34, EMDR 30; the adequacy of these courses is not reported).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 34 (interpretation gap): Table 1 can neither support nor refute that most participants had had first-line trauma-focused therapy; 'but not for' should read 'cannot be checked for'.
disagreements.resolution: Checked MAPP1's Table 1 on the publisher's table page (CBT 34, EMDR 30, prolonged exposure 1, none 2). Corrected.
